@graph.name: Combined Move-and-Store Operations
@graph.description: Combined move-and-store operations: a move with a storage interval between move-out and move-in, run as one coordinated plan — survey, quote, pack, load, intake, hold, redelivery, placement, reassembly, unpacking, and a final walkthrough. The move side is the published residential pattern: whole-home and apartment moves of every size; loading, transport and unloading; furniture protection and careful placement; disassembly and reassembly of standard furniture, planned up front; full, partial, or fragile-only packing plus unpacking at the other end; white-glove care for antiques and high-value pieces; custom crates when a piece needs more than padding. Where a move includes a high-mass asset of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, that piece moves under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation with L/360 floor-deflection analysis, as part of the same flat-rate move. The hold side, on the company's confirmed terms: items are held in leased storage between move-out and move-in, for any type of items — including containers, household goods, and machines such as robotic arms — with a 30-day minimum stay; customers can access their stored items while stored; lease terms vary; then goods are redelivered and placed room by room when the destination is ready. The quote path: one flat price in writing before move day for the job, through Get My Flat Rate Quote — the Short (Quick Quote) form by default or the Detailed Project form, switching in place with From, To and What's moving preserved — or the free film-only video walkthrough survey room, where the customer films and a person makes the estimate; nothing is auto-priced. Domain facts, labeled as such: a mover-held gap move typically involves two handlings against four for a self-storage gap; the condition recorded at intake is mirrored at release; redelivery is triggered by destination readiness, not by the calendar alone.

@graph.name: Storage Interval & Access Operations
@graph.description: Storage interval and access operations — the reference bands every move-with-storage plan is built from. Company terms, confirmed and published: the minimum stay is 30 days; customers can access their stored items while stored (no notice period, access hours, or attendant rule is published, because none was stated); lease terms vary, so no single uniform arrangement is claimed. Interval bands, as domain reference: a gap hold of days to weeks (closing gaps, overlapping leases); long-term holds of months to years (renovations, deployments, downsizing, estate transitions, staging); and storage-in-transit inside a move contract, a federally defined domain form capped at 180 days, after which goods convert to permanent storage under a separate warehouse contract with written notice — domain rules, published as education. The company does not claim storage-in-transit qualification: a regulator rule in the domain record (NCUC) requires SIT shipments to be held in a carrier-owned warehouse or a public warehouse under a long-term lease, and this company's storage is leased storage with varying lease terms, so the qualification is not established and is not claimed. Access models in the wider industry, labeled domain: business-hours access; advance notice of 24 or 48 hours in published examples; attendant-assisted access, sometimes at an hourly rate; partial retrieval of selected items, sometimes for a small handling fee — industry models listed for understanding, none of them published as this company's rule; the company's own published access term is the sentence above. Self-storage anytime access and portable-container driveway limits are domain comparisons, never company offers.

Duration bands: gap (days to weeks), the storage-in-transit window (to 180 days, domain), and long-term (months to years). The company's published item scope stands alone and is not a suitability table: any type of items — including containers, household goods, and machines such as robotic arms. No company accepted-items or prohibited-items list is published: the exclusions other movers commonly publish (perishables, live plants and animals, flammables, fuel and chemicals, illegal substances, unlicensed firearms, hazardous materials) are domain education only, recorded in the protection and compliance dataset as industry practice, never as this company's list. Climate, as domain rationale: stable temperature and humidity protect wood furniture, electronics, books, photographs and fabrics, and climate-controlled space is a standard industry form; no climate claim is made for the company's leased space. Specialty pieces are cross-referenced, never duplicated: pianos and antiques to the piano and antique category, safes and high-mass pieces to SIR and gun-safe moving, crates to custom crating, and freight staging to the industrial and commercial warehouse floor — a different service from household storage, never blurred with it.

@graph.name: Commercial Terms & Cost Drivers
@graph.description: Commercial terms and cost drivers for moving and storage. The company's confirmed terms are few and are stated exactly: the move is quoted at one flat rate in writing before move day, with no hourly meter; storage is quoted per job, monthly, or by volume — that is the pricing basis, and no rate, range, minimum charge beyond the stated 30-day minimum stay, fee, or deposit is published anywhere in this dataset; the minimum stay is 30 days; customers can access their stored items while stored; lease terms vary. Everything else here is domain education, researched and labeled, never company terms. Cost drivers in the industry: the volume held (home size, cubic feet, vault count), the duration of the hold, warehouse handling in and out, valuation coverage, and redelivery distance. Storage-in-transit terms in the federal framework (domain): a 180-day cap, then conversion to permanent storage under a separate warehouse contract with written notice covering the conversion date, a 9-month claim window, the end of transit liability, and the warehouseman's rules; under SIT, goods stay under the bill of lading and the move's valuation — Released Value at $0.60 per pound, with Full Value Protection available — and SIT rates are typically weight-based, billed in 30-day increments, sometimes prorated. Valuation is not insurance; it is a tariff-based level of carrier liability, and no valuation-during-hold term is published for the company. Published industry figures, from other movers and listed for education only: SIT at $0.40 to $0.75 per cubic foot per month plus about $75 per vault in each direction (one Florida source); vault storage at $85 to $115 per vault per month (one California source); $85 per vault per month plus a $100 setup fee (one Massachusetts source); monthly pricing by home size from one New Jersey mover (studio $130 to $250, two-bedroom $250 to $400, three-to-four bedroom $400 to $650); self-storage 5-by-10 units at $60 to $220 depending on market and climate control. No figure in this dataset is The Flat Rate Movers' price. Booking guidance in the industry: gap moves are commonly booked about 4 to 6 weeks before move-out day as a safe target.

@graph.name: Buyer Personas & Trigger Events
@graph.description: Buyer personas and trigger events for moving and storage — the buyers are people whose two dates stopped lining up. Closing-gap movers: the sale closes on one date and the purchase on another, and the hold bridges the gap. Renovators: the work finishes after move-out, and the household waits in storage. Downsizers and estate transitions: sorting what fits takes longer than the move itself, cross-referenced to the senior category, which owns its claims. Staged movers: moving in phases, holding part of the household between stages. Seasonal and temporary-housing holders: a posting, a school term, or travel holds the household between homes. Commercial stagers: inventory, fixtures, and FF&E held between leases or mid-build-out. Long-distance window movers: a delivery window on either end of a long-distance move creates the interval, cross-referenced to the long-distance category. The seasonal pattern is industry research, labeled as such: roughly 60 to 70 percent of US moves happen May through September, month-ends peak, and gap moves cluster around closings, which cluster around month-ends. Booking behavior is domain guidance: gap moves are commonly planned about 4 to 6 weeks ahead, and last-minute summer gaps face tighter availability. Every persona plans through the same published path: the Short or Detailed quote form with inputs preserved while switching, or the free film-only video walkthrough survey room with a human-made estimate — film only, never lift, move, open, or climb anything heavy or locked. Published branch hours are the branches' hours; no storage hours are claimed.
